summary:
A truck can only be slowed by trucks ahead of it, and a whole convoy arrives when its front truck does. So sort
trucks nearest-to-depot first and remember the arrival time of the convoy just ahead: a truck that would arrive
later than it can never catch up and starts a new convoy; otherwise it joins. Compare times by cross-multiplying,
in 64-bit, so they stay exact. O(n log n).

question.md:
Trucks on a one-lane road drive toward the depot. Each has a start mile and a speed. A faster truck that catches
a slower one ahead can't pass, so they continue together at the slower speed as a convoy. Catching up exactly at
the depot still counts. Return the number of convoys that arrive.

- **Positions are distinct**, but times can tie: a tie means "caught up exactly at the depot" and counts as
  one convoy.
- **Times are fractions** `(depot − position) / speed`. Distances and speeds go up to 10⁶, so cross-products
  reach 10¹²: they need 64-bit integers.
- **Up to 10⁵ trucks.**

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- Catching up exactly at the depot still joins the convoy.
- A truck already ahead and slower slows everyone behind it.
- Arrival times are fractions; compare `dist₁ · speed₂` with `dist₂ · speed₁` to stay exact.

think.md:
**Let new items collide with the top.** In these processes a new item only ever interacts with the **most recent
survivors**: the comet just to its left, the truck just ahead, the plate on top. A stack holds the survivors so far,
and each new item fights the top until it either wins (pop and continue) or stops. Every item is pushed and popped at
most once: O(n).

**Process trucks from the one nearest the depot.** A truck can only be held up by trucks ahead of it. Going from
the front of the road backwards, keep the arrival time of the convoy just ahead. A truck that would arrive **no
later** (on its own) catches up and joins that convoy; a truck that would arrive later is slower than everything
ahead, so it leads a new convoy. Depot at 12:

approaches.title: Compare with every truck ahead

idea.md: A truck leads its own convoy exactly when no truck ahead of it would arrive at the same time or later. Check that for every truck against every truck ahead.

build: For each truck, compare with every truck ahead.
Count trucks that no truck ahead holds up.

lines.text: Number of trucks that lead a convoy.
Truck `i`, its distance to the depot, and an assumption that it leads.

notes.java: Distances are `long` so the products below don't overflow.
notes.cpp: Distances are `long long` so the products below don't overflow.

lines.text: A truck ahead that arrives no sooner (`d_j/s_j ≥ d_i/s_i`, cross-multiplied to stay exact) means `i` will be held up.
No truck ahead is in the way: `i` leads its own convoy.

steps.text: Truck at mile 10 arrives at 1 h alone; every truck ahead arrives sooner (there are none). It leads a convoy.
Truck at mile 8 (alone: 1 h) is held up by the truck at mile 10 (1 h). It joins a convoy.
Truck at mile 0 arrives at 12 h alone; every truck ahead arrives sooner. It leads a convoy.
Truck at mile 5 arrives at 7 h alone; every truck ahead arrives sooner. It leads a convoy.
Truck at mile 3 (alone: 3 h) is held up by the truck at mile 5 (7 h). It joins a convoy.

walk.title: For every truck, check every truck ahead of it. It leads its own convoy only if every truck ahead would reach the depot strictly sooner.

limits.md: Compares every pair. After sorting by position, only the convoy just ahead matters.

approaches.title: Sort, then carry the latest arrival time

idea.md:
Sort trucks by position, nearest to the depot first. Keep the lead convoy's `(distance, speed)`. A truck
starts a new convoy when its arrival time is strictly later, compared exactly as
`dist · lead_speed > lead_dist · speed`.

build: Carry the latest convoy arrival time.
Count trucks that arrive strictly later.

lines.text: Trucks nearest to the depot first: each truck is only affected by those before it in this order.

notes.java: Each truck is packed into one `long` (position in the high bits, speed below 2²⁰), so a plain sort orders by position; we then walk from the end (nearest first).
notes.c: Positions are distinct, so the comparator only needs positions; their difference fits in an `int`.

lines.text: No convoy ahead yet, which is like one that arrives at time 0 = 0/1.
Each truck's distance to the depot.
`dist/s > leadDist/leadSpeed`, cross-multiplied (both denominators are positive). Strictly later means it never catches up; a tie means it catches up exactly at the depot and joins.
A new convoy, and its front truck's time is now the one any truck behind must beat.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** for the sort. **Space O(n).**

steps.text: Sorted nearest-first, with each truck's arrival time if it drove alone.
Mile 10: 1 h > 0 h, so it never catches the convoy ahead. New convoy; the time to beat becomes 1 h.
Mile 8: 1 h ≤ 1 h, so it catches the convoy ahead exactly at the depot and joins it.
Mile 5: 7 h > 1 h, so it never catches the convoy ahead. New convoy; the time to beat becomes 7 h.
Mile 3: 3 h ≤ 7 h, so it catches the convoy ahead and joins it.
Mile 0: 12 h > 7 h, so it never catches the convoy ahead. New convoy; the time to beat becomes 12 h.

walk.title: Sort by position, nearest to the depot first. Keep the arrival time of the convoy just ahead; a truck that would arrive later starts a new convoy.

takeaways.md:
- **Car fleets:** sort by position from the front; a slower-arriving truck starts a new fleet.
- Compare fractions by cross-multiplication.
- **Pitfall:** floating-point arrival times with exact ties.
